summary: Updates RFC 2418 to give working group chairs explicit responsibility for managing their mailing lists. In particular, chairs may temporarily suspend the posting privileges of disruptive individuals. It was replaced by RFC 9945.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3934 updates the rules for managing IETF working-group mailing lists. It lets a chair temporarily suspend a disruptive person's ability to post, while keeping that person able to receive messages.

can a working group chair suspend posting
subtitle: A working-group chair can temporarily suspend disruptive mailing-list posting.

tldr.problem: RFC 2418 gave working-group chairs authority to manage disruptive behavior in meetings but required full IESG approval to suspend mailing-list posting privileges.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3934 updates RFC 2418 so a chair can suspend posting as a last resort, usually after warnings and consultation with the Area Director, for no more than 30 days.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3934 updated RFC 2418 and was later obsoleted by RFC 9945.

today: RFC 3934 updated RFC 2418 and has been obsoleted by RFC 9945.

sections.title: The Mailing-List Management Gap
sections.content:
RFC 2418 gave working-group chairs authority to manage disruptive behavior during face-to-face discussions. It did not give them the same authority over mailing-list discussions and required full IESG approval to suspend someone's posting privileges.

RFC 3934 updates Section 3.2 of RFC 2418 to let a chair temporarily suspend posting privileges without that approval.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier rules let chairs manage disruption in meetings but not directly on mailing lists. This update gives them a limited way to address repeated disruption online.

sections.title: Warnings Before a Suspension
sections.content:
Unless severe behavior must stop immediately, the chair should first contact the individual directly. If the behavior continues, the chair should send at least one public warning to the working-group list.

As a last resort, usually after one or more explicit warnings and consultation with the responsible Area Director, the chair may suspend posting privileges for no more than 30 days. The person must still be allowed to receive list messages, and the decision may be appealed under RFC 2026.
sections.plainLanguage: The chair normally contacts the person privately, then warns them on the list if the behavior continues. A suspension is a last resort and does not block the person from reading messages.

sections.title: Limits on the Chair's Authority
sections.content:
The procedure allows only short suspensions. A chair cannot use it to suspend posting for more than 30 days, regardless of the incident's type or severity. Further disruptive behavior is considered separately and may lead to additional warnings or suspensions.

Longer suspensions and other forms of list control must follow other IETF-approved procedures. The RFC identifies BCP 83 as one existing set of procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: This procedure cannot be used for a suspension longer than 30 days. Longer restrictions must follow a different IETF-approved process.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC describes this change as a modification to IETF process for managing mailing-list discussions. It says the change has no security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC treats this as a process change and identifies no security considerations.
